description: Charge transfer, electric fields, current, potential difference, resistance, Ohm's law, and I-V characteristics.
content_html:
Static Electricity

Charge is a fundamental property of all matter. In most objects, the number of positive charges equals the number of negative charges, so the object is electrically neutral. When two insulating materials are rubbed together, friction causes electrons to transfer from one surface to the other, creating static electricity.

The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. It is always the electrons that move — protons are locked inside the nucleus and cannot transfer between objects. For example, when a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons move from the cloth to the rod: the rod becomes negative and the cloth becomes positive.

Static charge builds up only on insulators because electrons cannot flow away through the material. On a conductor, any excess charge spreads out immediately. If enough charge accumulates, it can discharge as a spark — this is what causes lightning.

Key Fact

Static electricity is caused by the transfer of electrons between insulating materials. An object becomes positive by losing electrons — not by gaining positive charges. Protons never move between objects.

Electric Fields

A charged object creates an electric field in the space around it. Electric field lines show the direction a positive charge would move if placed in the field — they point away from positive charges and towards negative charges. Where field lines are closer together, the field is stronger.

Two charged objects exert forces on each other through their electric fields — like charges repel and unlike charges attract. This force acts even without the objects touching, which is why a charged balloon can attract small pieces of paper without contact.

Current, Charge and Potential Difference

Current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor. For current to flow, there must be a source of potential difference and a complete (closed) circuit. The equation linking charge, current and time is:

$$Q = I \times t$$

Where \(Q\) is charge (coulombs, C), \(I\) is current (amperes, A), and \(t\) is time (seconds, s). In a series circuit, current is the same at every point because charge is not used up. Current is measured with an ammeter in series; potential difference is measured with a voltmeter in parallel across the component.

Resistance and Ohm’s Law

Resistance opposes the flow of current. The greater the resistance, the smaller the current for a given potential difference. The relationship is:

$$V = I \times R$$

Where \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (Ω). Ohm’s Law states that current is directly proportional to potential difference, provided temperature remains constant. This applies only to ohmic conductors — components whose resistance stays constant.

Key Fact

\(V = IR\) links potential difference, current and resistance. Ohm’s Law: current is proportional to PD only if temperature is constant (ohmic conductor). Current measured by ammeter in series; PD by voltmeter in parallel.

Set up a circuit with a variable resistor, ammeter in series, and voltmeter in parallel across the component under test. Adjust the variable resistor to change the current; record both current and potential difference at each setting. Plot an I-V graph (current on y-axis, potential difference on x-axis). For a resistor at constant temperature, the graph is a straight line through the origin — confirming Ohm’s Law. Repeat with a filament lamp and a diode to compare their I-V characteristics.

I-V Characteristics

An I-V characteristic graph shows how current varies with potential difference for a component. You need to know the shape for three key components (PAG P7):

• Fixed resistor (ohmic conductor): a straight line through the origin. Gradient is constant, so resistance is constant. Obeys Ohm’s Law.
• Filament lamp: an S-shaped curve that starts steep (low resistance when cool) and flattens as PD increases (higher resistance as the filament heats up). As current increases, the filament temperature rises, so resistance increases. The curve is symmetrical in forward and reverse directions.
• Diode: current only flows in one direction (the forward direction). In the reverse direction, resistance is very high and virtually no current flows. There is a threshold voltage (roughly 0.6 V for a silicon diode) below which even forward current is negligible.

Some components have resistance that changes with environmental conditions:

• A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has high resistance in the dark and low resistance in bright light. Used in automatic streetlights and burglar alarms.
• An NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot. Used in thermostats, fire alarms, and engine management systems.
Both are used in potential divider circuits where their changing resistance produces a varying output voltage that depends on light level or temperature.

Key Fact

I-V graph shapes: resistor = straight line (constant resistance, obeys Ohm’s Law); filament lamp = curve (resistance increases with temperature); diode = conducts in one direction only.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about static electricity, always state that electrons transfer — never protons or positive charges. For I-V graph questions, explain the shape by linking it to resistance and temperature (for the lamp) or the one-way nature of current flow (for the diode). For calculation questions using \(V = IR\), always identify which value you are solving for and rearrange the equation before substituting numbers. A common error is using the wrong value for current when the ammeter is in parallel — remember, the ammeter must always be in series.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Static electricity is caused by electron transfer between insulators. Only electrons move — positive charges never transfer. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. Charge creates an electric field in the surrounding space.
  • Current (A) = charge (C) ÷ time (s). Resistance opposes current. Ohm’s Law: \(V = IR\) applies when temperature is constant. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.
  • I-V graph shapes: fixed resistor = straight line; filament lamp = S-curve (resistance increases with temperature); diode = one-way conduction only. LDR and thermistor resistance changes with light and temperature.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following explains why a polythene rod becomes negatively charged when rubbed with a woollen cloth?
A) Positive charges transfer from the cloth to the rod
B) Electrons transfer from the cloth to the rod
C) Protons transfer from the rod to the cloth
D) Electrons transfer from the rod to the cloth
practice_questions.marks:
B) Electrons transfer from the cloth to the rod [1 mark]
Electrons move from the cloth to the rod, giving the rod extra electrons and therefore a negative charge. Protons never transfer; positive charges do not physically move.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by resistance in an electrical circuit.
practice_questions.marks: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current through a component, measured in ohms (Ω). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A component has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a resistance of 30 Ω.
Calculate the current through the component.
practice_questions.marks:
Identify equation: V = IR, so I = V ÷ R [1 mark]
Substitute: I = 12 ÷ 30 [1 mark]
I = 0.4 A [1 mark]
Unit: A (amperes) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the I-V characteristic of a filament lamp. Explain why the graph has this shape.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes a curve that starts steep and flattens as PD increases (not a straight line). Explains that as more current flows, the filament heats up, increasing resistance. Higher resistance means less current flows for each additional unit of PD, so the graph flattens. [3 marks]
Secure: Correctly describes the shape as a curve and states resistance increases with temperature, but does not link temperature rise to increased current. [2 marks]
Developing: States the graph is a curve but does not explain why. [1 mark]
Emerging: Describes a straight line — incorrect. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates the resistance of a length of resistance wire. She measures the potential difference across the wire and the current through it at five different settings of a variable resistor. The results give a straight line through the origin on an I-V graph.
Explain what the student can conclude from this result.
practice_questions.marks: The wire is an ohmic conductor [1 mark] because current is directly proportional to potential difference (Ohm's Law holds), which means resistance is constant and temperature has not changed significantly during the experiment [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of a diode and an LDR as components in an automatic night light circuit that switches on when it gets dark. For each component, explain its role and any limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: LDR — resistance increases in the dark, providing a higher voltage signal that can trigger the circuit to switch on. Diode — ensures current flows only in one direction, protecting other components from reverse current damage. Limitations: LDR sensitivity threshold needs calibrating; diode has a forward voltage threshold (~0.6 V for silicon) below which it won't conduct; LDR response time may lag rapidly changing light conditions. Both components are cost-effective and reliable for this application. Justified conclusion on overall suitability. [5–6 marks]
Secure: Correct role for both components, some limitations mentioned. [3–4 marks]
Developing: Correct role for one component only. [1–2 marks]
Emerging: Minimal relevant physics. [0 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: A student rubs a glass rod with a silk cloth. The glass rod becomes positively charged. What has happened?
options: Protons have moved from the silk to the glass rod
Electrons have moved from the glass rod to the silk
Positive charges have moved from the silk to the glass rod
Electrons have moved from the silk to the glass rod

knowledge_checks.q: Which component has a resistance that decreases when light intensity increases?
Current is measured using an ammeter connected in _____ with the component.
For an ohmic conductor, current is directly proportional to potential difference provided _____ remains constant.
Match each component to its I-V characteristic:
right: Straight line through origin — constant resistance
S-shaped curve — resistance increases with temperature
Conducts in one direction only — near-zero reverse current

flashcard_questions.q: Why does rubbing a polythene rod make it negatively charged?
flashcard_questions.a: Electrons transfer from the cloth to the rod, giving it excess electrons.
A build-up of charge on an insulating material caused by electron transfer through friction.
A region around a charged object where another charge experiences a force.

flashcard_questions.q: State the equation linking charge, current and time.

flashcard_questions.a: Current through a conductor is proportional to PD, provided temperature is constant.

flashcard_questions.q: What equation links potential difference, current and resistance?
Describe the I-V graph for a diode.
flashcard_questions.a: Conducts only in the forward direction; nearly zero current in reverse.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a filament lamp's I-V graph curve and not remain straight?
flashcard_questions.a: As current increases, the filament heats up, increasing resistance.

flashcard_questions.q: How does resistance in an LDR change as light intensity increases?
flashcard_questions.a: Resistance decreases as light intensity increases.

flashcard_questions.q: How is a voltmeter connected to measure potential difference across a component?
How is an ammeter connected to measure current?
flashcard_questions.a: In series within the circuit branch.

glossary_terms.definition: A property of all matter. There are two types of charge — positive and negative. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.
A build-up of charge on the surface of an insulating material, caused by the transfer of electrons through friction.
A region of space around a charged object where another charged object experiences a force.
The rate of flow of charge (electrons) around a circuit, measured in amperes (A).
The energy transferred per unit charge across a component, measured in volts (V). Also called voltage.
A measure of how much a component opposes the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω).
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature remains constant. This applies to ohmic conductors only.
A graph of current (I) against potential difference (V) for a component. The shape shows whether the component obeys Ohm's law and how its resistance changes.
